entries.title: Poland says Starlink station fire 'act of sabotage'
entries.summary: Polish Deputy Prime Minister Krzysztof Gawkowski said Warsaw believed the attack aimed to disrupt internet access for the Ukrainian military, calling it "an element of the next phase of hybrid warfare."
entries.content:
Poland

Poland says Starlink station fire 'act of sabotage'

September 24, 2026

Polish Deputy Prime Minister Krzysztof Gawkowski said Warsaw believed the attack aimed to disrupt internet access for the Ukrainian military, calling it "an element of the next phase of hybrid warfare."

Warsaw considers a fire that broke out at a Starlink station in central Poland to be an act of sabotage, Deputy Prime Minister Krzysztof Gawkowski said on Thursday.

"This act of sabotage was deliberately designed to disable the station ... disrupting internet access for various institutions, including the Ukrainian army," Gawkowski, who also serves as digital minister, told public broadcaster TVP.

He said the fire at the station belonging to Polish state-owned telecom company Exatel broke out late on Wednesday.

"There is much to suggest that we are dealing with an element of the next phase of hybrid warfare," he said.

The deputy premier said that the station was used to transmit internet traffic through Poland, including to neighboring Ukraine.

He also said there were "many indications" suggesting the incident "fits into this new Russian doctrine of attack."

Poland accuses Russia of 'hybrid' warfare

Poland and other EU and NATO member states have accused Russia of engaging in hybrid warfare, including acts of sabotage, against Ukraine's allies, since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.

Lying on the EU and NATO's eastern flank, Poland borders Ukraine, the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad and Moscow ally Belarus. It is one of Kyiv's strongest supporters in Europe.

Warsaw also joined the new "Carpathian Eight" regional summit launched by Ukraine last Friday.

Earlier in September, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned that Russia plans to carry out "hybrid" drone and missile strikes against Ukraine's allies.

Late last year, Poland accused Russia of carrying out "state terrorism" over an act of sabotage on the Polish rail network.

entries.title: Morocco: Center-right PAM leads in parliamentary election
entries.summary: PAM is part of Morocco's outgoing ruling coalition and was founded by an adviser to the king. The moderate Islamist Justice and Development Party surged amid increasing voter apathy.
entries.content:
Morocco

Morocco: Center-right PAM leads in parliamentary election

September 24, 2026

PAM is part of Morocco's outgoing ruling coalition and was founded by an adviser to the king. The moderate Islamist Justice and Development Party surged amid increasing voter apathy.

Morocco's center-right Authenticity and Modernity Party (PAM) took first place in Wednesday's parliamentary election, according to provisional results.

PAM is part of Morocco's outgoing ruling coalition.

The party won 97 out of 395 seats in parliament, 10 seats more than in 2021.

It was founded in 2008 by an adviser to the king and advocates social modernization and moderate secularist views. It is largely seen as close to the Moroccan monarchy.

The next coalition government will oversee preparations for the 2030 World Cup.

The vote is not expected to fundamentally alter the balance of power in the North African kingdom. As the country is a semi-constitutional monarchy, Morocco's King Mohammed VI retains substantial powers in both policy direction and foreign affairs.

How did other parties fare in Morocco's election?

The National Rally of Independents (RNI), the senior partner in the outgoing coalition, dropped from 102 to 66 seats, putting it at second place.

The smallest member of the governing coalition, the right-wing Istiqlal party also saw losses, taking 65 seats, 16 fewer than in 2021.

The moderate Islamist opposition Justice and Development Party surged to 54 seats, compared to just 13 in 2021.

Election marked by increasing voter apathy

The election saw turnout of 38%, marking the lowest level since 2007. Nearly 16 million people were registered to vote.

Only around 4% of registered voters were aged 18 to 24.

In 2025, Morocco was rocked by Gen Z-led protests, which were the largest in the country since the Arab Spring in the early 2010s.

Mistrust in politicians and issues regarding living conditions were widely blamed for the low turnout.

"I'm not going to vote because I have lost all faith in the political class," 50-year-old Majda Bakatir told the AFP news agency.

"We want our country to move forward, but politicians do not seem to care about our problems regarding healthcare, education, and purchasing power," she said.

entries.title: Germany news: Bundestag to discuss opt-out organ donation
entries.summary: Parliamentarians debate whether to change Germany's organ donation scheme amid a lack of supply. They will also consider reforms to expand the power of intelligence agencies. DW has more.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Bundestag to discuss opt-out organ donation

Published September 24, 2026last updated September 24, 2026

Parliamentarians debate whether to change Germany's organ donation scheme amid a lack of supply. They will also consider reforms to expand the power of intelligence agencies. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Lawmakers debate whether to introduce an opt-out scheme for organ donation
  • The Bundestag will also examine government proposals to grant intelligence agencies a wider scope to counter manifold security threats
  • German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has warned of Russia's growing aggression against Europe
  • The first-ever Islamic theology faculty in Germany is to open in Münster

Here is a roundup of the top news stories from and about Germany on Thursday, September 24, 2026:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.

Skip next section 105-year-old suspected Nazi POW guard under investigation

105-year-old suspected Nazi POW guard under investigation

German prosecutors said on Thursday that they were investigating a 105-year-old man over crimes that might have been committed during his alleged time as a guard at a Nazi prisoner-of-war camp during World War II.

In a statement seen by the AFP news agency, they said the man was "thought to have been a guard at the prisoner-of-war camp Stalag 326 VI K" in the Senne region of western Germany.

The man is "accused of being an accessory to multiple murders through his activities there," the statement said.

The Stalag 326 VI K camp held between 180,000 and 200,000 Soviet prisoners of war between 1941 and April 1945, when it was liberated by US troops, according to the memorial at the site.

Some 30,000 Soviet POWs are believed to have died at the camp.

The age of the suspect is a reminder that time is running out to prosecute people who committed crimes as part of Germany's Nazi regime.

In April 2025,  for example, an alleged former guard at the Sachsenhausen concentration camp near Berlin died before he could face trial on charges of complicity in the murder of more than 3,300 people.

Skip next section Berlin officially withdraws Olympics bid

Berlin officially withdraws Olympics bid

Berlin has confirmed reports that it is withdrawing its bid to host the Summer Olympics and Paralympics.

The decision means that only Munich and the western Rhine/Ruhr region are still in the running as potential hosts, with Hamburg having pulled out in May after failing to win support at a referendum. 

The withdrawal comes after the socialist Left Party's victory in Berlin's elections on Sunday. The party's lead candidate and potential mayor, Elif Eralp, said she did not support Berlin's bid.

The current mayor, Kai Wegner of the conservative Christian Democrats (CDU), told reporters: "Today is a sad day for Berlin, because the Olympic and Paralympic Games would have been a tremendous opportunity."

"When Ms. Eralp stated that the bid was effectively off the table ... the leading sports associations made it clear: We cannot give you our approval under these circumstances," he said, adding: "I deeply regret this."

Kaweh Niroomand, the volleyball manager who led the Berlin bid, said, "We simply could not offer the political stability required."

On Saturday, the German Olympic Committee (DOSB) is to choose a preferred region as part of a bid to the International Olympic Committee to host one of the 2036, 2040 and 2044 Summer Games.

The Summer Olympics have been held twice on German soil.

Berlin hosted the Games in 1936 in then Nazi-ruled Germany and Munich, then as part of West Germany, was the site of the 1972 Games.

Skip next section IN DEPTH: Top economic think tanks raise 2026 GDP growth forecasts

IN DEPTH: Top economic think tanks raise 2026 GDP growth forecasts

Economic experts predicted on Thursday that German GDP will double to 1.3% this year. They also warned of difficulties ahead.

You can read more about their forecasts for Germany's economic future in the next few years in this article: Germany: Economic institutes double growth forecast for 2026

Skip next section Planned intelligence reforms trigger heated Bundestag debate

Planned intelligence reforms trigger heated Bundestag debate

The German parliament has held its first debate on government plans to give intelligence agencies more power as national security is threatened by new dangers at home and from abroad.

Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt told parliamentarians that the planned reforms would turn Germany's intelligence agencies — the BND (Bundesnachrichtendienst), in charge of international intelligence, and the BfV (Bundesamt für Verfassungschutz), responsible for domestic intelligence — into "true secret services."

He said the agencies would no longer just gather information on threats but be equipped to provide "real defense against dangers, attacks and terror."

Under the plans, the agencies would receive more power to collect, save and automatically evaluate data, as well as permission to react to sabotage or hacking attacks with counterattacks.

Intelligence reforms under fire

Various parliamentarians voiced concerns about the reform's implications in what was sometimes a heated discussion.

Konstantin von Notz from the Green Party said he recognized the need to "update" the powers of the agencies in view of the growing threat from Russia.

But, he said, "the excessive plans for domestic intelligence activities" needed to be trimmed or the the reforms would not survive an appeal to the Constitutional Court.

He said the government needed to take the interests of people professionally entrusted with confidential information much more into consideration, especially psychotherapists.

Clara Bünger of the socialistLeft Party accused the government of breaking down the distinction between intelligence agencies and the police that had been a lesson learned "from the crimes of the German fascists."

The far-right politician Gottfried Curio from the Alternative for Germany (AfD) party was strongest in his criticism, saying the government wanted to create a "Stasi 2.0," a reference to the secret service in former communist East Germany.   

The reforms would bring about "more than a total surveillance state," he said.

Skip next section Bundestag set for organ donation debate

Bundestag set for organ donation debate

The Bundestag will discuss two separate cross-party proposals on Thursday to increase the number of human organs donated for often life-saving transplant operations.

One proposal upholds Germany's current system, under which people who wish to donate organs must actively give permission.

Advocates of the proposal say that the shortfall of donated organs can be remedied by campaigns calling on adults to take part and making it easier to register the desire to donate.

The other proposal calls for an opt-out scheme under which organs can be removed postmortem from anyone who has not expressly rejected being an organ donor.

Backers of this proposal say that although surveys show that most people in Germany are willing to donate their organs, very few actually document this wish.

They also cite statistics showing that countries with opt-out schemes have more donations, with Germany lagging behind in international comparisons.

Altogether 254 of the 630 members of the Bundestag have signed on to the opt-out scheme, and 58 have backed the first proposal to maintain the current national system.

The Bundestag last voted on the issue in 2020, with a majority supporting the opt-in model, even though an opt-out proposal had more signees then, too.

France, Spain and the Netherlands are examples of European countries that have opt-out models in place.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

The DW newsroom in Bonn says guten Tag and willkommen to its readers around the world!

You join our coverage as the German parliament is set to revisit a debate on organ donations: Should an opt-out scheme replace the current opt-in one in view of the dwindling supply?

Parliamentarians will also be looking at goverment proposals to give more powers to the country's intelligence agencies to enable them to cope with the current myriad of security threats.

And the university in Münster is to open a faculty of Islamic theology — the first in the country — that will have an equal status with the Catholic and Protestant faculties there.

All this comes amid a bit of good news for the German economy, which experts say will grow twice as much this year as previously forecast.

Read on for more on these and other stories.

entries.title: Germany: Economic institutes double growth forecast for 2026
entries.summary: Experts predict German GDP will double to 1.3% this year but warn of structural difficulties ahead. The picture is complicated, they say, especially because of uncertainty in the energy sector.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany: Economic institutes double growth forecast for 2026

September 24, 2026

Experts predict German GDP will double to 1.3% this year but warn of structural difficulties ahead. The picture is complicated, they say, especially because of uncertainty in the energy sector.

Several leading German economic think tanks on Thursday announced they had increased their earlier GDP growth forecasts for the country.

New numbers predict an uptick of 1.3% for 2026, more than double that of spring forecasts of 0.6% growth.

In their so-called "Autumn 2026 Joint Economic Forecast," this year titled "Recovery Under Structural Stress — Fiscal Policy on Slippery Ground," five institutes also adjusted their economic outlook for 2027, predicting 1.1% growth.

The picture looks less rosy in 2028, when GDP is expected to slow to just 0.4% growth.

"The economy saw more robust development than expected," said Oliver Holtemöller of the Leibniz Institute Halle (IWH). "Still, that upturn rests on a rather wobbly foundation because high energy prices and structural problems continue to be a burden."

Experts say that the trend is clear but add that recovery is nevertheless weaker than in the past.

Analysts said a strong global economy and the AI boom had in part fueled the trend but added that corporate investment and private consumption remained weak.

Structural problems, uncertainty persist

Looking ahead, economists say they expect dynamism in 2027 as consumer spending recovers and housing construction gains pace.

German institutes are not alone in their positive forecast. The Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) — a group of mostly rich countries — also adjusted its forecast to 1.1% growth in Germany's GDP this year, up from 0.7% in June.

Additionally, the OECD foresees 1.1% growth for Germany in 2027.

One thing that all observers agree on — beyond the need for urgent long-term reforms — is that the US-Israel-Iran war in the Middle East and the great uncertainty that the conflict brings to the global economy is the biggest wildcard in the deck.

Despite the cautious optimism voiced in Thursday's report, many economists have warned that increased government spending on infrastructure and defense — largely financed through new debt — could quickly become a flash in the pan if not coupled with sustainable reforms.    

In Berlin, Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who has shown himself to be committed to pushing those reforms through the Bundestag, also recently voiced a bit of optimism over Germany’s economic future, saying, "We're out of the valley of economic recession or decline."

The five institutes that issued the Joint Economic Forecast are: the German Institute for Economic Research, the IfO Institute, the Kiel Institute for Global Economics, the Leibniz Institute for Economic Research Halle and the RWI-Leibniz Institute for Economic Research Essen.

entries.title: India news: 9 killed after bus catches fire outside Delhi
entries.summary: At least nine passengers were killed after a sleeper bus caught fire on the Yamuna Expressway in Greater Noida, near India's capital Delhi. DW has more.
entries.content:
India

India news: Cockroach party demands election head resign

Published September 24, 2026last updated September 24, 2026

CJP's Abhijeet Dipke has alleged that the removal of more than 130 million names from draft electoral rolls is designed to benefit the BJP and weaken opposition parties. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Cockroach Janata Party founder Abhijeet Dipke accused Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar of undermining the country's democracy
  • Dipke called Kumar "the biggest threat to India's democracy" and demanded his resignation
  • Fire on sleeper bus kills nine outside of Delhi
  • This is the latest in similar incidents of deadly fires on buses
  • SIT files chargesheet in Ayodhya Ram Temple donation theft case
  • Three arrested over alleged gang rape of minor girl in New Delhi

Here are some of the major headlines from India on Thursday, September 24:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section Three arrested over alleged gang rape of 17-year-old girl in New Delhi

Three arrested over alleged gang rape of 17-year-old girl in New Delhi

Authorities have arrested three men accused gang-raping a 17-year-old girl in southeast Delhi.

The girl had been visiting a temple with a male friend on Monday evening before the two went to a nearby park, where the suspects allegedly intercepted them. The men posed as police officers to intimidate the minor and her friend.

One of the men reportedly restrained the girl's friend while the other two assaulted her.

The suspects allegedly threatened the pair with arrest if they reported the incident, according to police cited by The Hindustan Times.

On Wednesday, ​hundreds of students protested in Delhi, demanding better safety for women. The alleged assault occurred barely 2 km (1.2 miles) from Lady Shri Ram (LSR) College, one of the country's top women's colleges.

India has a high rate of reported sexual violence against women and girls. National Crime Records Bureau data shows that more than 80 rape cases are reported to police across the country each day.

Skip next section SIT files chargesheet in Ayodhya Ram Temple donation theft case

SIT files chargesheet in Ayodhya Ram Temple donation theft case

An investigation team probing the alleged embezzlement of donations and offerings at the Ram Temple in the northern city of Ayodhya has filed a chargesheet against eight arrested suspects, media reports said on Wednesday.

The police filed a 74,000-page chargesheet before a local court. All eight accused are in judicial custody.

The Special Investigation Team's (SIT) status report documented 105 instances of theft captured by CCTV cameras at the temple premises.

The controversy over alleged embezzlement  forced authorities to appoint an Indian Air Force veteran, Jeetendra Mishra, as the chief executive officer of the temple earlier this month.

The construction of the temple, inaugurated by Prime Minister Narendra Modi in January 2024, was a longstanding political issue and a key commitment of Modi's nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

It built at the site of the Babri mosque, which was demolished by Hindu nationalist mobs in 1992.

Devout Hindus believe that the god Ram was born there more than 7,000 years ago, but that the Babri mosque was built over his birthplace by a 16th-century Muslim emperor.

Skip next section Fire on sleeper bus kills nine outside of Delhi

Fire on sleeper bus kills nine outside of Delhi

Nine passengers were killed late on Wednesday after an overnight sleeper bus caught fire outside of the national capital, New Delhi, according to media reports.

A police report, cited by the media, said the bus' air conditioning unit caused the fire while on the Yamuna Expressway in Greater Noida.

Police added that the bus driver and conductor managed to escape the fire and are detained by the authorities, according to The Times of India newspaper.

A passenger who managed to escape the tragedy told ANI news agency that the bus was packed with passengers.

"I was sleeping when someone woke me up saying the bus had caught fire, and we all scrambled to get out," the passenger said. "It was not an easy situation to escape, there was a lot of smoke. We somehow managed to get out."

The police are investigating the incident.

This is the latest in similar incidents of deadly fires on buses:

  • March 2026: At least 13 people died in a bus accident in Andhra Pradesh
  • October 2025: At least 20 people died after a bus caught fire following a collision with a motorcycle in Kurnool, Andhra Pradesh
  • October 2025: A bus fire in Rajasthan killed at least 20 people and left around 16 others seriously injured
  • April 2025: At least 25 people died and eight others were injured after the bus they were traveling in caught fire on an expressway in Maharashtra

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Hi, this is Shakeel from DW's New Delhi studio bringing you the latest updates from across India.

Nine passengers were killed late on Wednesday when their overnight sleeper bus caught fire just outside Delhi.

Meanwhile, a Special Investigation Team (SIT) filed a nearly 70,000-page chargesheet against eight people arrested in connection with the Ram Temple donation embezzlement case on Wednesday.

For all this and more, follow our live blog.

entries.title: US judge blocks Trump ban of CNN, MS NOW, Politico from White House, orders him to restore access
entries.summary: A judge has ordered President Trump to restore White House access to CNN, MS NOW and Politico after he banned the media outlets from the premises.
entries.content:
United States of America

US: Judge orders Trump to lift White House media ban

September 24, 2026

A judge has ordered President Trump to restore White House access to CNN, MS NOW and Politico after he banned the media outlets from the premises.

​A federal judge on Thursday said US President Donald Trump must lift his ban on journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico accessing the White House.

The ruling came in response to a lawsuit filed by the news organizations contesting the ban, issued on September 18.

In his order, District Judge Tim Kelly said the ban was likely unconstitutional.

Kelly said his order must remain in place for 14 days.

"This is a strong ruling vindicating freedom of the press, due process and the rule of law," Theodore Boutrous Jr., attorney for the outlets, said in a statement emailed to the AP news agency. "We greatly appreciate the court’s swift action."

What did the judge say about the ban?

Kelly rejected the government's claim that national security concerns promoted the ban.

"The record lacks factual support for defendants’ contention that the revocation of plaintiffs' hard passes will ​in fact protect national security or that national security will be endangered if the court orders their passes reinstated while this litigation ​proceeds," he said.

He pointed out that Trump himself had initially cited only an "alleged lack of truthfulness and negativity" in reporting by the outlets as the reason for the ban.

At a Wednesday hearing, Kelly said two previous rulings from the US Court of Appeals for the ⁠District of ​Columbia Circuit had established that White House press passes can be revoked only after due process.

He said the banned news outlets did not appear to have been given a proper chance to contest the ban.

Kelly, who was nominated by Trump in 2017, ordered a CNN journalist’s access restored in a similar case in 2018.

The ban led other media outlets, including DW, to take action in solidarity by suspending pooled coverage of Trump events.

Department of Justice support for ban

On Tuesday, the Justice Department had argued in a filing that access ⁠to the White House was a privilege, not ​an entitlement, and that the president had the authority to deny access news organizations.

The outlets, in turn, argued they were singled out because of the content of their coverage and called the ban a "blatant violation" of the First Amendment, which prevents government infringement on freedom of speech and freedom of the press in the United States.

entries.title: OpenAI agent hacked Australia government portal: PM Albanese
entries.summary: The hack of Australian health data marks the world's first known AI-led breach of a government website.
entries.content:
September 24, 2026

The hack of Australian health data marks the world's first known AI-led breach of a government website.

An OpenAI agent infiltrated an Australian government health data portal, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said Thursday, in what is the first known instance of an artificial intelligence hack of a government system.

Albanese said the breach occurred in June when an autonomous OpenAI program accessed both "public and non-public" files on the statistics reporting portal of Medicare — Australia's publicly funded universal health insurance scheme.

The available evidence did not indicate a broader network compromise, Albanese said, adding, "Nonetheless, this situation is obviously unacceptable."

Albanese said he spoke to OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman to express Australia's "extreme concern" over the incident.

OpenAI, the developer of ChatGPT,  said in a statement that it spotted the breach while carrying out an "extensive review" of its AI tools, adding that "our models took actions we did not intend".

Altman had earlier on Wednesday addressed the UN Security Council, apprising the risks AI poses as the world faces the technology's development.

What did Australia's Albanese say about the OpenAI breach?

Albanese told reporters that OpenAI informed Australia about the breach only on September 10, three months after the incident, through an email sent to a public mailbox.

The Australian leader said he expressed his "disappointment" to Altman that it took OpenAI "way too long to inform the government" on what occurred.

Albanese also deemed the nature of the notification "unacceptable."

The prime minister announced that a probe into the security breach would determine whether OpenAI could face criminal charges.

He added that the investigation would also examine how the breach went past Australia's security agencies, which were unaware of it before OpenAI notified them.

How did the breach take place?

The breach occurred as OpenAI ran training exercises to rate the performance of AI models.

Government Services Minister Katy Gallagher said OpenAI asked the model to search the internet for data showing how much Australia's government spent on medicine.

She said the portal had since been closed and the data moved to more secure systems.

Albanese said no personal information is believed to have been accessed during the incident.

"I think OpenAI know that they need to have better protocols in place. And they're one of the businesses that themselves have warned of the risks which are there," Albanese said.

What has OpenAI said?

OpenAI said in its statement that it discovered the rogue activity in an August review.

"During this review, we identified activity involving several Australian government websites and services as our models attempted to look up answers and available statistics for questions about Australia during an internal evaluation," it said.

The San Francisco-based company added that it had found no evidence of Australian patient records being accessed.

Australia's Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles called the breach "fundamentally unacceptable."

"It was not sitting behind a particularly high fence. This AI agent scaled the fence ... and the point is it was unintended. It wasn't asked to. That's our concern here," Marles said.

In July, OpenAI disclosed that its advanced AI model went rogue during a security test and carried out a dayslong hacking spree into the Hugging Face AI technology digital repository.

Days later, rival company Anthropic announced that three separate versions of its AI broke out of cybertesting environments and hacked three firms.

Edited by: Sean Sinico

entries.title: Germany sets out plan to phase out fossil fuels by 2045
entries.summary: Germany sets out a plan to phase out coal, oil and gas by 2045, reaffirming a climate strategy focused on electrification.
entries.content:
September 24, 2026

Germany sets out a plan to phase out coal, oil and gas by 2045, reaffirming a climate strategy focused on electrification.

Germany has presented a roadmap to phase out fossil fuels by 2045.

Germany's Environment Minister Carsten Schneider told the UN General Assembly on Wednesday that the plan "combines independence, affordability, and climate protection."

Europe's largest economy is now the third country to have provided a solid plan for the phaseout — to which nearly 200 countries committed at the 2023 COP28 climate conference in Dubai — following France and the Netherlands.

What did Berlin say about the fossil phaseout plan?

Schneider, of the center-left Social Democratic Party, said the decision was linked to the Iran war and its impact on fuel supplies worldwide.

"It is not just extreme weather events around the world that demonstrate how urgently we need to do more to protect the climate," he said. "If the situation in the Strait of Hormuz determines whether people can still afford their daily commute to work, that is not a good state of affairs."

He said he believed the 19-year deadline was feasible.

"Our roadmap is intended to set an international example. I am sure that many other countries will follow."

Schneider said that fossil fuels accounted for 65% of Germany's energy consumption in 2024.

The majority of that — 98% of its oil and 95% of its natural gas — was imported at a cost of €76 billion ($86.5 billion). The minister stressed that the figure has since risen sharply due to the Iran war.

How have environmental organizations reacted to the plan?

Several environmental organizations welcomed Berlin's plan, though some highlighted that it contradicted some recent government decisions.

"With this announcement, Germany is showing a sign of life in international climate policy," said Greenpeace energy expert Mira Jäger.

However, she noted that "at the same time, the federal government is subsidizing the oil industry, breaking the heating transition, and slowing down the expansion of renewables."

Fentje Jacobsen, a climate policy advisor at the World Wide Fund for Nature, argued that the roadmap largely rehashed existing initiatives without adding "new ideas or additional ambitions."

"The current government is meanwhile planning to rely less on renewables and more on gas," she added.

Energy Minister Katherina Reiche of the conservative Christian Democrats has advocated building new gas-fired power plants, arguing that this would help stabilize the electricity grid and highlighting the intermittent nature of renewable sources such as wind and solar.

Reiche has also demanded preserving a larger role for combustion-engine vehicles using alternative fuels, a position that contradicts the phaseout plan, which foresees battery-electric cars accounting for 100% of new passenger car registrations by 2035.

Germany's car industry is a pillar of the country's economy, and the recent struggles it has faced have naturally been reflected in the broader economy.

Edited by: Roshni Majumdar

entries.title: Trump welcomes China's Xi for high-stakes summit
entries.summary: Donald Trump welcomed Xi Jinping to the US by greeting him personally on the tarmac at Joint Base Andrews. The two are expected to discuss trade, AI, Taiwan and Iran during a three-day state visit.
entries.content:
United States of America

Trump welcomes China's Xi for high-stakes summit

Published September 24, 2026last updated September 24, 2026

Donald Trump welcomed Xi Jinping to the US by greeting him personally on the tarmac at Joint Base Andrews. The two are expected to discuss trade, AI, Taiwan and Iran during a three-day state visit.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Donald Trump welcomed his Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping, to Washington for a multi-day state visit
  • This is Xi's first state visit to the US in a decade
  • Trade, AI, Taiwan, Ukraine and Iran are key issues to be discussed

Follow along here for live updates on Xi's state visit to the US:

Skip next section We're pausing our coverage for now

We're pausing our coverage for now

The main summit between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping is scheduled for Thursday.

There's a state dinner as well in the evening, with both leaders expected to deliver speeches.

Top US tech executives are expected to attend the dinner, suggesting that artificial intelligence will be a big topic of discussion.

Skip next section China, US should be 'partners rather than rivals' — Xi

China, US should be 'partners rather than rivals' — Xi

Chinese President Xi Jinping has called for cooperation with the US, Beijing's state news agency Xinhua reported.

"Our two countries should be partners rather than rivals," Xi said in a written statement published by Xinhua.

"The Chinese and US peoples have enjoyed long-standing friendly exchanges, and our interests are deeply intertwined," Xi added.

Xi was welcomed in Washington with a red carpet and military flyover.

In remarks published by Xinhua, Xi also said he looked forward to "in-depth exchanges" with Trump on "major issues concerning our bilateral relations and the global situation."

Skip next section Trump wants Hong Kong's Jimmy Lai to be freed from prison — report

Trump wants Hong Kong's Jimmy Lai to be freed from prison — report

Chinese President Xi Jinping has arrived in Washington to a rare planeside welcome from his US counterpart, Donald Trump. 

As Xi walked down a long red carpet on the airport tarmac, a White House spokesperson said that Trump believes Hong Kongdemocracy advocate Jimmy Lai should be released from prison and "wants to see that happen," the DPA news agency reported.

"The United States urges the authorities to grant Mr. Lai humanitarian parole," DPA quoted the spokesperson as saying.

Lai, a 78-year-old media tycoon, was sentenced to 20 years in prison earlier in the year under the National Security Law that China imposed in 2020 following massive pro-democracy protests in Hong Kong. 

At a congressional hearing in Washington last week, Lai's son, Sebastien, repeated his appeal for his father's release.

Trump raised the issue of Lai's release when he met Xi in Beijing in May, but the US leader said the Chinese president told him Lai's case "would be a tough one."

On Tuesday, US outlet Politico reported that British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has asked Trump to discuss the release of Lai, who is a British citizen, with Xi.

Skip next section US, China to extend trade truce through January 2, Scott Bessent says

US, China to extend trade truce through January 2, Scott Bessent says

The US and China have agreed to extend their trade truce by two months, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said.

The announcement came as Chinese President Xi Jinping arrived in Washington to meet with US President Donald Trump.

"We have agreed today that we will extend what we call the Busan Agreement, the economic detente between the two countries that was scheduled to end on November 10th," Bessent told Fox News.

The extension of the one-year trade truce buys both sides more time to negotiate.

Skip next section IN PHOTOS: Trump welcomes China's Xi to United States

IN PHOTOS: Trump welcomes China's Xi to United States

Skip next section Trump hosts Xi in Washington: What to expect

Trump hosts Xi in Washington: What to expect

Chinese President Xi Jinping's plane landed in Washington for his state visit to the US, which will include a meeting and state dinner with  Donald Trump on Thursday.

Unlike with other leaders, Trump honored Xi by welcoming him at Joint Base Andrews outside Washington rather than waiting for him at the White House.

The greeting, which included a red carpet lined by US service members and a military flyover, kicks off the Chinese leader's three-day visit to Washington.

Additional fanfare during the trip is due to include a state dinner with tech executives and a visit to the National Archives, where the original Declaration of Independence and Constitution are housed.

Expectations for a breakthrough during Xi's visit were slim.

Despite their deep disagreements, the two world leaders went ahead with their summit that analysts say is meant to project stability on the world stage.

The issues the two will discuss are expected to include trade, artificial intelligence, as well as the wars in Iran and Ukraine.

Xi will also likely press Trump on Taiwan, a topic Washington would prefer to avoid, while Trump will likely maintain firm US export controls despite Xi's objections.

Welcome to our coverage

We are launching our coverage of the highly anticipated meeting between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington.

Trade, the wars in Iran and Ukraine, and artificial intelligence are expected to be on the agenda as the two leaders hold their main meeting on Thursday.

This is Xi's first state visit to Washington in a decade.

Germany

Berlin Airport briefly suspends flights over drone sighting

September 23, 2026

Airspace over the German capital was closed for about 45 minutes after a drone was spotted on the runway. Flights have resumed but are experiencing delays.

Berlin's airport briefly suspended flights on Wednesday evening after a drone sighting, Germany's DPA news agency cited airport and police officials as saying.

A drone was spotted on the Berlin Brandenburg Airport's northern runway at 8:00 p.m. (1800 GMT). Airspace above the airport was closed minutes later and operations were suspended for at least 45 minutes.

Several flights were diverted to Dresden.

As of 9:05 p.m., airspace was reopened but flights were experiencing delays.

Drone sightings on the rise

Drone sightings have become a common occurrence for airports in Europe, with Berlin's airport recording the highest number of sightings in Germany in the first part of the year.

Some 28 drone sightings were recorded during the first six months, as per figures by the German air traffic control (DFS). In seven of those cases, flight operations at the airport were temporarily suspended.

This is a jump from last year, when eight drones were detected at the airport and its surroundings in the whole of 2025, according to DFS.
